prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is a clean case of a quantitative theoretical prediction (the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model, 2011) followed years later by a decisive experiment (correlated insulators and superconductivity, 2018) and then by reproduction in many independent laboratories. It opened moire flat-band physics as a tunable platform for strongly correlated electrons, a genuine new quantum behaviour in a material. It also connects to what I care about: first-principles and model theory checked against transport and spectroscopy, and an echo of graphene itself, where experiment overturned what theorists thought possible. Having listened to colleagues, I now put it ahead of my opening first choice. The attribution for B022 is cleaner than for B054, because the theory and experiment halves map onto three named people without a glaring hole, and three of five opening ballots (Mehlig, Olsson, Pearce) already converge on the Bistritzer, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero trio.
statement.case_against: The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity and the nature of the correlated insulators are still unresolved, so the theory side of the story is not settled and some will say the prize is early. Twist-angle disorder and sample-to-sample variation remain reproducibility concerns. Credit is also incomplete: Yuan Cao and the other first authors of the 2018 papers cannot be named, and earlier twisted-graphene band theory (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) could be argued as a precursor. If the committee judges that interpretation must settle before recognition, B054 (very mature, stable interpretation) or B036 (mature, broadly confirmed metrology) is the safer choice.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B022 first as a model-first discovery in which a simple mechanism, moire interference flattening the bands, was quantitatively tested and opened a field, and he supports the theory-plus-experiment trio including Bistritzer.
responses.response: I agree with this and it moves me. In my opening I proposed only MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, thinking the two-person split cleaner. I now accept that Bistritzer is the first author of the 2011 flat-band prediction and that leaving him out would be hard to defend on attribution grounds. I still want to ask more than you do about robustness: a flat band predicted at the magic angle is verified, but the superconducting state is not explained by that model, so the citation should be worded around the prediction and the observed phases, not around a mechanism.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks (B036) first as the clearest case of a measurement technique opening new ways of observing nature, mature, reproduced in many laboratories, with the redefinition of the second pending.
responses.response: I take the maturity argument seriously and I list B036 among my alternatives, because reproducibility across independent laboratories is exactly the criterion I apply. My qualification is that the new physics rewarded is less a discovery than a long refinement of metrology, with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-trap prize already adjacent, which you partly acknowledge yourself. I am also uneasy that you suggest waiting for the SI redefinition; the discovery should stand on its own merit. I would rank B036 as a strong but incremental candidate. Moire flat bands are a new state-of-matter platform, so I would weigh them higher.

responses.point: Johansson ranks B054 only sixth, noting that the 2016 topological-phases prize already covered part of the conceptual ground and that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 3D topological-insulator work are missing from the credited names. He ranks B022 last of the shortlist because the discovery is recent and the mechanism unsettled.
responses.response: Your attribution point on B054 is correct and I concede it. I ranked B054 first, but the credited trio omits the BHZ prediction that the HgTe experiment actually tested, so the allocation is weaker than I allowed in my opening. I do not accept the 2016 overlap as decisive: that prize honoured topological phase transitions and the integer quantum Hall-type phases, whereas Z2 time-reversal-invariant topology is a distinct class. On B022 I disagree about prematurity. The 2018 phases have been reproduced by many groups over eight years, and the unresolved mechanism did not stop us from rewarding other correlated-electron discoveries, so I keep B022 ahead of B054 but would not object to B054 as a close second choice.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron microscopy (B021) first as the decisive instrument advance enabling single-atom imaging and spectroscopy in materials physics, while ranking B022 third and B054 fourth.
responses.response: I share your respect for the instrument: much of the experimental spectroscopy that my theory is checked against depends on it. My reservation is the same one you raise, that Knut Urban's role in the first corrected TEM is unresolved with only three names allowed, and that an instrument prize leaves the physics discovery less central. B021 had a single first-place vote and no other ranking, so I do not see it as the strongest basis for the prize this year, but I would want a careful archival check of the priority before dismissing it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept recognising twisted bilayer graphene before the superconducting pairing mechanism is understood.
How to handle the uncredited 2018 first authors (Cao and colleagues) and earlier twisted-graphene theory, given the three-person limit.
Whether B054 should be preferred because its experimental record is more mature, despite the missing BHZ credit and the possible 2016 overlap.
I recall the dates and priorities from memory and have not verified them against the record.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I work in theoretical magnetism and electronic structure at Uppsala, with no stated tie to the candidates named on B022, B054 or B036.
